evidence.title: Implementation of a clinical decision support tool for hypertension in a rural health system
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: BP remeasurement and hypertension recognition, high- vs low-intensity implementation support
evidence.effect: High-intensity (in-person/online training, monthly check-ins, feedback) vs low-intensity (online training only): remeasurement 51.5% vs 23.6%, aOR 3.45 (1.88-6.33); recognition 42.8% vs 24.5%, aOR 2.31 (1.08-4.98).
evidence.quote: High-intensity implementation was more effective than low-intensity implementation for repeat BP measurement (aOR 3.45; 1.88-6.33) and hypertension recognition (aOR 2.31; 1.08-4.98).

evidence.title: AI adoption and workflow optimization following orchestration platform implementation and structured change management
evidence.outcome: Radiologist user-verification rate of AI outputs
evidence.effect: Combined structured change management (education, standardization, feedback, governance) and platform associated with verification increasing from 13.9% to 61.1%; uncontrolled pre-post, bundled intervention.
evidence.quote: In conclusion, a combined orchestration platform and change management strategy was associated with substantially increased AI adoption and integration into routine neuroradiology workflow.

evidence.title: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Clinician Experiences and Adoption Patterns of an EHR-integrated Generative AI-based Clinical Decision Support in Kenya
evidence.outcome: Clinician adoption of LLM decision support under structured change management
evidence.effect: AI Consult use across 16 facilities rose from 4% to 47% over 8 months; 21.7% of 258,106 episodes used it. No comparator without change management.
evidence.quote: It is possible to achieve non-trivial adoption of GenAI-based CDSS (4% to 47% over 8 months) when supported by structured change management.

evidence.title: Nuclear medicine technologists practice impacted by AI denoising applications in PET/CT images
evidence.outcome: Perceived facilitators and barriers to implementing an AI denoising PET/CT algorithm
evidence.effect: Focus group participants named explanations and available support such as a "local champion" as main facilitators; lack of education, workflow challenges and professional resistance were main barriers.
evidence.quote: The main barriers to implement this algorithm included workflow challenges, resistance from professionals and lack of education; while the main facilitators were explanations and the availability of support to ask questions such as a "local champion".

commentary.bottom_line: One cluster randomized trial found that high-intensity implementation support (training, monthly check-ins, and feedback) was associated with higher rates of target clinical actions than online training alone, and a descriptive study and a focus group point the same way. The trial record does not state that the tool was AI, and no study isolated a funded change team or champion role, so this recommendation rests on low-certainty evidence.

perspectives.view: The cluster trial (n=9155 patients) reported remeasurement of 51.5% vs 23.6% (aOR 3.45, 1.88-6.33) and recognition of 42.8% vs 24.5% (aOR 2.31, 1.08-4.98). Certainty drops for indirectness, because the record does not describe an AI tool, and for imprecision. The Kenyan study lacks a comparator, and the focus group reports perceptions only.

In 16 Kenyan facilities under structured change management, AI Consult use rose from 4% to 47% over 8 months, and 21.7% of 258,106 episodes used it. Without a comparison group, the rise may reflect time or familiarity. Ten Swiss technologists named explanations and a local champion as facilitators, and lack of education and workflow problems as barriers.

The trial measured clinician actions, remeasuring blood pressure and recognizing hypertension. This suggests that more intensive support may help a tool catch problems that clinicians would otherwise miss. No study measured patient harm, errors, or overreliance, so the effect of champions on safety events remains untested.

The high-intensity arm required in-person and online training, monthly check-ins, and feedback, which implies staff time beyond a single online course. None of the three studies reported cost, staffing levels, or champion time, so a health system cannot estimate from this evidence the budget needed to reproduce these results.

The trial enrolled rural patients, and the descriptive study ran in Kenyan facilities. No study reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Whether champion-led support changes use of AI tools in clinics serving these patients is unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared an AI deployment with and without a funded change-management team or designated champion while measuring adoption, appropriate use, clinician expectations, cost, and patient outcomes. A cluster randomized or stepped-wedge trial across sites, including safety-net clinics, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: The one trial included rural patients. None of the three studies reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The findings may not transfer to settings with thinner staffing, where funding a champion role competes with other needs.
